_README: This file holds ALL the words shown to participants. You can edit any text
below and the change appears in the app after you save this file and refresh
the browser. No coding and no rebuild are needed.
How to edit safely:
1. Only change the text INSIDE the double quotes, for example the part after
a label like "title": "...edit this...".
2. Keep every quote, comma, colon and curly brace exactly where it is. If the
page goes blank after an edit, you most likely deleted a quote or comma.
3. To make a word bold, wrap it in **double stars**. For italic, use *single
stars*. Example: "You will read **16 emails**, one at a time."
4. Words inside curly braces such as {role}, {name} or {total} are filled in
automatically by the app. Leave the braces and the word inside them as is.
Write {article} (or {Article} at the start of a sentence) for the 'a'/'an'
before {role}; the app picks the right one, e.g. 'an Executive Assistant'.
5. Lines starting with an underscore, like this _README, are notes for you
and are never shown to participants.
Compensation and timing live in instructions.compensation below.
Job areas are stored with readable names, so they show as-is. Optional
on-screen renames live in clusterLabels. Each assigned role's title and
description live in the roles section, keyed by the job area name.

app._progressNote: The small label next to the progress bar at the top of every page. 'screening' covers the pages up to the recap. 'scenarios' is the eight-situations page: it gets its own label because that page is the first half of the paid task, and labelling it 'Getting started' told participants the real work had not begun. In 'email', {n} and {total} are filled in automatically.

clusterLabels._note: Optional display overrides. Left side = the exact value stored in the database, right side = what participants see on screen. The job areas are already stored with readable names, so no overrides are needed. Add an entry here only if you ever want to show a different label for one.

instructions.title: About this study
instructions._whatYouDoNote: Each item can be a plain string, or an object with a 'main' line, a 'sub' list of nested points, and an optional 'tail' line shown after that list. Edit the text inside the quotes only; keep the braces { } and words like {role} as they are. Use {article} for the 'a'/'an' before {role} (it is filled in automatically as 'a Sales Executive' or 'an Executive Assistant'). Name the three factors ONCE, in the sub-list of the first step, and use its 'tail' to say what to do with them. Listing them a second time as 'what you are judging' only reads as repetition, since the participant has already met them on the landing page.

whatYouDo.main: Being {article} {role}, you will look at **eight work email scenarios**. Each one is a different combination of three things:
sub: **Who sends it**: a senior colleague, or a peer or junior one.
**How urgent it is**: with a priority, or with no rush.
**What is at stake**: a reward for doing the task, or a consequence for not doing it.
whatYouDo.tail: For each scenario you rate **how realistic** that combination is for {article} **{role}**, weighing the three together rather than one at a time. The question is always whether **that sender** is in a position to send you that message, not whether the email is well written.

whatYouDo.main: Then read **16 emails**, one at a time: two written for each of those eight scenarios. For every email you will:
sub: rate **how realistic** it is, and say why in a sentence or two,
if something does not feel right, edit the email in place to make it more realistic.

compensation._note: Shown as a highlighted strip on the About page: a reassurance line on the left, then two stat tiles (time and pay). Edit only the text inside the quotes.
compensation.note: There are no right or wrong answers, just your honest judgement.

consentText: Participation is **voluntary**. You may withdraw at any time by closing the tab, and your responses will not be submitted.
Your **Prolific ID** is collected only to pay you. After the study it is **detached from your responses**, so the data is made anonymous and used solely for academic research.
You will type free text when you rate and rewrite the emails. **Do not include any personal names (yours, colleagues', or a manager's) or company names**.
instructions.consentCheckbox: I have read the information above and I consent to take part in this study.

clusterSelect._note: The landing page. The study is invitation-only and every invited participant already gave us their job area and job title in the screening survey, so this page CONFIRMS both back to them instead of asking. Neither is editable: a participant whose job has changed since the screening survey is caught by the fit question further down, which is the one that matters for the task.
clusterSelect.title: Email realism validation
clusterSelect.lead: Thank you for taking part. You will take on a work role close to your own and judge whether the emails that role receives could realistically come from the people who send them.
clusterSelect.confirmHeading: This is what you told us in the screening survey
clusterSelect.confirmHelp: You were invited to this study on the basis of these answers, so we have carried them over for you.
clusterSelect.confirmNote: If either of these is wrong, please message us through Prolific before going on.

prolific.title: Your Prolific ID
prolific.lead: Please enter your Prolific ID exactly as it appears in your Prolific account, so we can match you to the screening survey you completed earlier.
prolific._note: Only seen by a participant who arrives without the ?PROLIFIC_PID= parameter Prolific normally adds to the study URL. Everybody else is matched automatically and never sees this page.
prolific.invalidHint: That does not look like a Prolific ID. It is 24 letters and numbers.

blocked.notInvitedTitle: This study is by invitation only
blocked.notInvitedBody: This study was sent to a specific group of people who completed our earlier screening survey, and this Prolific ID is not one of them. If you typed your ID in by hand, please check it and try again. If it is correct, please return the submission on Prolific so it goes back to somebody who was invited, and message us if you believe you were invited and are seeing this in error.
blocked.completedTitle: You have already completed this study
blocked.completedBody: Our records show that this Prolific ID has already finished the study. Each person can take part only once, so there is nothing more for you to do here. If you believe this is a mistake, please message us through Prolific.
blocked.clusterTitle: This Prolific ID is registered for a different job area
blocked.clusterBody: This Prolific ID is already part-way through the study for the **{cluster}** job area, which is not the area we now have on record for you. To keep the study valid, each participant stays with the area they started in. Please message us through Prolific and we will put it right.
blocked._note: Three refusals. NOT_INVITED is the only one that offers a way forward (a mistyped ID at manual entry), so it is the only one with a button. CLUSTER_LOCKED should be unreachable now that the job area is assigned rather than chosen; it shows only if the roster is regenerated mid-study.

role.title: You are assigned with a job role for this task
role.lead: For the rest of the study, please **imagine** you are the person described below, working inside a **large company** with many departments (finance, IT, HR, sales, operations and more).
role._rolePrefixNote: Goes in front of the assigned role in the highlighted panel, giving 'Imagine you are an Executive Assistant'. Keep the 'imagine' in it: this line is the one thing a participant who skims the page is certain to read, and without it the line states that they ARE that role rather than asking them to play it.
role.relHeading: How does your own job role (**{ownRole}**) compare to the assigned role (**{role}**)?

relOptions.label: About the same level: a peer of {article} {role}

role._taskExplainerNote: The most important block on the landing page. A pilot showed participants judged the CONTENT of the emails (whether the task made sense, how it was written) instead of whether that sender, pressing that hard, holding out that reward or consequence, is in a position to send such an email to that role. The block therefore names the WRONG thing to judge before it names the right one ('contrast' below: a Not row and a But row), because people who have already started reading for content need that misreading interrupted, not just a positive instruction. Two rules when editing: (1) NEVER add worked examples or say which combinations are realistic. Telling people that, say, a junior would not warn you about a consequence teaches them a rule and they stop judging: a junior can legitimately warn that something will be escalated and hit you both. The 'factors' below are deliberately written as QUESTIONS about the sender's standing, never as answers. (2) Keep it short, or people skip it.

taskExplainer.eyebrow: Please read this before you continue
taskExplainer.heading: What we mean by a realistic email
taskExplainer.lead: The emails are already written, and we are not checking spelling, wording, or whether the task itself is a sensible piece of work. What we need your judgment on is whether the sender, given their position relative to {article} **{role}**, could realistically send that message at all.
taskExplainer._contrastNote: Two rows shown side by side, the wrong question first and the right one second. Keep them as a pair: the first row is what pilot participants did by default, and seeing it named is what makes the second row land.

contrast.label: Not
contrast.text: Is this a well written email, and is what it asks for reasonable?

contrast.label: But
contrast.text: Is **this sender** in a position to ask me this, to press me like that, and to put that at stake?

factors.label: The sender
factors.text: Would a person at their level be the one sending this to {article} **{role}**?

factors.label: The urgency
factors.text: Would they press for it that hard, or put it that casually?

factors.label: What is at stake
factors.text: Would they hold out a reward, or point to a consequence, in that way?

taskExplainer.closing: Take the three as one picture, not one at a time: **could this particular sender really send me this type of email?**
taskExplainer.note: There is no right answer. Some combinations will feel perfectly normal to you and others will not, and we want your honest read either way.

role.fitTail: We are asking for your **expert opinion** on who sends what to {article} **{role}**, and on what terms. You do not need to have held this exact job, but it should be familiar enough for you to judge that.
role.fitQuestion: Do you feel you know this kind of role well enough to judge who could realistically send it these emails, and in what way?
role.fitConfirmButton: Yes, I understand the task and know this role
role.fitDeclineButton: No, this is not a good fit for me
role.exitTitle: This study may not be a good fit
role.exitText: Thank you for your honesty. This study needs people who can judge, from their own working experience, who would realistically send these emails to the role shown and how. No data has been saved and you have not consented to anything.
role.exitProlificNote: Please return your submission on Prolific so it can be offered to someone else.
role.exitProlificButton: Take me back to my Prolific

checks.heading: Quick checks
checks.intro: A few quick questions to confirm the task is clear. The emails only make sense once you are picturing yourself in the role.
checks._note: For each question, 'answer' is the number of the correct option, counting the options from the top starting at 1. Keep the correct option and 'answer' in sync if you reorder them.

questions.prompt: For the rest of this study, who should you imagine you are?
options: Myself, in my own current job
A customer writing in to the company
A job applicant hoping to be hired

questions.prompt: When you rate each email, what are you mainly judging?
options: Whether the email has spelling or grammar mistakes
Whether the task it asks for is a sensible piece of work
Whether a sender at that level could realistically send an email like this to {article} {role}
Whether the email is polite enough

questions.prompt: To judge whether an email is realistic for your role, you weigh up whether a sender at that level, with their authority, would...
options: be the one sending you the email in the first place
send the email with the mentioned level of urgency
offer any reward, or hold out consequences for not doing it
All of the above, weighed together

checks._feedbackNote: After a failed attempt, the answer the participant chose is marked with a green tick or a red cross. Only their own answer is marked: the correct option is never revealed on a wrong one, or the retry would stop being a comprehension check. correctLabel and incorrectLabel are not shown on screen: they are read out by screen readers, so the marks are not colour alone.
checks.error: Not quite. Think again about your role, then choose again.

recapPoints: First, rate **how realistic** eight work email scenarios are for {article} **{role}**.
Then read **16 emails**, one per page, each addressed to you as {article} **{role}**, and rate **how realistic** each one is.
If **anything feels off**, use the **Edit** buttons to rewrite just those parts.
You can add an optional comment for each email.
recap.nameHeading: Pick a name for the emails
recap.nameLead: So the emails read naturally, each will greet you by a first name you choose (for example, *Dear Alex,*).
recap.nameWarning: Please do **not** use your own real name.
recap.nameFieldLabel: First name to use in the emails
recap.nameInvalidHint: Please enter a single first name using letters only.
recap.nameConfirmCheckbox: I confirm this is not my own real name.

_note: Shown once, right after the recap and before the 16 emails. Participants give their general expectation for eight everyday email situations BEFORE they have seen any of our example emails, so these are their un-primed judgments. The eight items are the 2x2x2 combinations of sender (more senior vs peer or junior), urgency (right away vs no rush) and framing (a problem to avoid vs a benefit to gain). Keep the wording plain and do NOT name those three factors on screen. The order is shuffled per participant automatically. 'key' is stored in the data and must not be changed; edit only the 'text'.

The title calls this the FIRST TASK on purpose. These ratings are study data, not a warm-up, and an earlier title ('Before you begin reading') made the page read as something to get past before the real work, which invites rushed answers. Keep the lead's 'before you read any of the emails' framing, since that is what makes these judgments un-primed, but do not retitle the page as a preamble.
priorJudgments.pageTitle: Your first task: the eight scenarios
priorJudgments.lead: Before you read any of the emails, we would like your **general expectation**. Below are eight everyday situations. For each, **tell us how realistic** it is that you, as {article} **{role}**, would receive an email like that at work **from the colleague described**. There are no right answers, and you have not seen our emails yet, so answer from your own experience of the role.
priorJudgments.requiredHint: Please rate all eight situations before you continue.
priorJudgments.closingLead: For each of these eight situations you will now see **two emails**, **16 in total**. For every email you will:
closingPoints: Say **why** in a sentence or two.
Optionally, **edit** anything that feels off to make it more realistic.

items.text: A **senior** colleague asks you to do a task **with a priority**, mentioning a **potential consequence** if you do not do it.
A **senior** colleague asks you to do a task **with a priority**, mentioning a **reward** if you do it.
A **senior** colleague asks you to do a task **with no rush**, mentioning a **potential consequence** if you do not do it.
A **senior** colleague asks you to do a task **with no rush**, mentioning a **reward** if you do it.
A **peer or junior** colleague asks you to do a task **with a priority**, mentioning a **potential consequence** if you do not do it.
A **peer or junior** colleague asks you to do a task **with a priority**, mentioning a **reward** if you do it.
A **peer or junior** colleague asks you to do a task **with no rush**, mentioning a **potential consequence** if you do not do it.
A **peer or junior** colleague asks you to do a task **with no rush**, mentioning a **reward** if you do it.

email.conditionsTitle: What to expect in this email
email._conditionsSentenceNote: IMPORTANT: the sentence shown under 'What to expect in this email' is NOT taken from here. It is copied word for word from the matching situation in priorJudgments.items above, looked up by this email's combination of sender, urgency and framing, so the participant reads the identical wording for the scenario they rated on the first-task page. To change that wording, edit priorJudgments.items. The template below is only a fallback, used if a combination has no matching situation there.
email.conditionsSentence: This email is from {dir}. It asks you to do a task {urg}, and mentions {frame}.
email.editBannerTitle: Keep your edits true to this email
email._editBannerSentenceNote: {situation} is filled in with the same word-for-word situation described above, so the reminder shown while editing matches what the participant read before editing.
email.editBannerSentence: Keep your changes in line with this email's situation: {situation}
email.editBannerWarn: The sender stays as shown. You can rephrase the request, its urgency and its framing so they fit what a sender at this level could realistically send. Please DO NOT turn it into a different kind of email.

conditions._note: The summary line at the top of each email is built from these parts and is worded to match the eight situations on the 'Before you begin reading' page. The template is conditionsSentence above: 'This email is from {dir}. It asks you to do a task {urg}, and mentions {frame}.' Keep the **bold** on the sender, the urgency phrase and the reward/consequence.

frame.threat: a **potential consequence** if you do not do it

email.questionsIntro: Now please answer the questions below about the email.
email.q1Heading: 1. Is this email realistic for your role?
email.q1Sub: Is **this sender**, at their level in relation to {article} **{role}**, in a position to send you this, to press you like that, and to put that at stake? Judge the three **together**, not one at a time.
email.q1Required: Please choose a rating to continue.
email.q2Heading: 2. In a sentence or two, why did you give that rating?
email.q2Sub: Tell us what made it feel realistic or not for {article} **{role}**, and say something about **the sender**: what someone at their level could or could not credibly ask, promise, or warn you about.
email.q2Required: Please add a short explanation for your rating to continue.
email.q3Heading: 3. Would you like to change anything to make it more realistic for **{role}**?
email.q3Sub: **Optional**. If something felt unrealistic for {article} **{role}**, use the edit option to reword it.
email.q3EditHint: You can now edit the subject and the message text above. The sender, the link, and the signature stay as they are. Click **Done editing** when you have finished.

done.title: Thank you
done.lead: Your responses for all 16 emails have been recorded. You can now return to Prolific to complete your submission.
done.completionHelp: Copy this code and paste it into Prolific, or use the button below to return to Prolific and submit it automatically.
done.completionMissing: Please return to Prolific to complete your submission.
